Off the grid

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Eskom runs out of money at the end of the month what happens then is anyones guess, but for those mavericks who are living off the grid they will barely notice - what does it take and is it an option

Summary:
Carte Blanche meets the early adopters who have gone off the grid and finds out if it is a good idea as the country faces a year of constrained supply

Further information:
Adios Eskom

At the end of the month Eskom will run out of money. Just how that will affect the country hardly bears thinking about, but there is a small group of people that probably wont even notice. They are the mavericks, the early adopters – those who have chosen to get off the grid and generate their own power. How did they do it? What did it cost them? As we look on from our darkened homes with envy, we wonder if we too can make the leap and say Adios Eskom!

Inus Dreckmeyr lives East of Pretoria in a beautiful home with his wife and family and all the creature comforts you can imagine. Six years ago he built him home, designed to keep warm in winter and cool in summer. He has custom built a solar array that moves with the sun, increasing his power by about 70 %. He has a room full of batteries which store the excess energy he will need at night and when they are full the energy diverts to a water pump that pumps borehole water to a tank on the hill to give the family enough water pressure for bathing and showering

At the time Inus spent around R600 000 to equip his home. But now as the cost of PV has dropped by about 80% he believes it will cost about half of that.

At the top of the hill overlooking Hartebeespoort dam is the property of the Henning family. The modest house that looks like it is painted with an Ndebele design is in fact a means to attract heat in winter and repel it in summer. This is the home of architect Professor Holm who went off the grid way back in 1974. His hot water comes from a glass encased black box that heats up and pushes itself into an insulated tank that provides the pressure for showering. But this fascination with solar runs in the family and his son Henning now spends his days helping big corporate clients reduce their dependency on Eskom. His office and home are flanked by Solar panels – in winter heated water runs under his floors giving him underfloor heating. Everything is connected via a computer so at any given time he can see exactly what is happening on the property. To power the three homes and a business he has built a mini grid with inverter and a roomful of batteries. It’s an impressive operation that has cost in the region of R900 000.
The business belongs to his brother in law, Paul, a blacksmith who makes beautiful cast iron art. Paul was fed up. He says he endured 28 days with no power in Hekpoort in 2014. His friends are selling up businesses and moving elsewhere. Paul decided to take his chance with solar and moved his forge onto the property recently. It’s a strange sight to see lumbering old German machines from the 30’s shaping red hot pieces of iron into beautiful artwork and remembering its all being powered from just a few solar panels on old man Henning’s rooftop.

But ask Henning Holm if we should get off the grid and he will tell you no, it’s still too expensive. What you should do is get a hybrid system he says. That way you can get the best of both worlds. He will explain this system to Derek.

But if you decide you want to make the leap and you don’t have R300 000 lying around what do you do? Will the banks lend a hand?

“ I used to have a round head, now its flat” says Brett Petzer who has spent the last four years knocking on the doors of the top four banks.“ They weren’t interested” he says and the green bank refused to cross the threshold. Nevertheless Brett has developed an off grid townhouse development in Midrand. “ The whites weren’t interested he said, but my black clients said this is the future and bought into the development and the concept” He will introduce us to Mr Stockbroker who runs everything in this stylish development off solar panels, except his Jacuzzi. And his bill from Eskom: Zero!

THE GERMAN EXAMPLE

As the Germans can show – living off solar panels not only provides enough for our own needs, there is usually plenty to spare. In an effort to go renewable the German government introduced incentives for their citizens to sell energy back to the grid and in so doing Germans put up solar PV panels everywhere.

They paid a lot for their energy, but in a few short years Germany has as much solar PV energy as the entire South African energy grid.

“ In terms of solar Germany decided they would buy a Mercedes S class because they wanted renewables even though they were expensive. As a result of that Germany pushed down the price of solar PV to such an extent that now South Africa can do the same thing but at the price of a VW Golf” that is the message from the CSIR’s Dr Tobias Bischoff Niemz.

Dr Bischoff Niemz is an expert in the field and is advising NERSA on how to do the same thing here. The exciting news for jaded Eskom customers is that last month NERSA issued a discussion document. Until now feeding energy into the grid has been illegal in South Africa. But as Eskom battles to keep the lights on NERSA is taking a tentative step towards opening up the market. Put up a system on your roof and you may either be able to sell on your excess energy or get credits for what you do use – thereby reducing your bill. It called net metering or NET FIT (FEED IN TARIFF)

But before you get too excited – it’s not yet law and there is a large and powerful lobby against this in the form of the municipalities and the METRO’S who Dr Bischoff Niemz says will go bankrupt if too many homeowners and businesses decide to ditch the grid.

A huge portion of the metro and munics revenue comes from the mark up on electricity, which is then used to cross subsidize other municipal functions. But the CSIR doctor has a plan. “ Don’t let this happen under the radar,” he says.

He suggests that a central purchasing agency buys your energy back at say 70cents per kwh. We import our electricity at about R1 30 per kwh. He also suggests that the agency guarantee a pay back for about 20 years, which will mean banks may lend to home owners knowing that they are likely to get their money back.

We need to do this right he says. If you do one thing wrong the whole thing can fail. In Spain the whole experiment failed because they did it wrong.

“ I am less excited about this net metering than others” says Peter Woodhatch an ex banker, skeptically. “ Say one invests in a lot of PV and then at a point government decides they don’t want your energy anymore. Then you lose your return on investment.”

Peter is another young maverick. His new home in Linden is built and designed to keep the temperature relatively constant and when Eskom said they wanted R20 000 for a connection from the street to his gate he decided to get off the grid instead. Peter was prompted by what he calls comfort. Too many friends and family members had spent hours fighting with ESKOM over ridiculous bills. He says he has neither time nor the will to spend hours fighting the city over incorrect billing. Peter has a gas geyser and stove and an electric oven. He has a neat row of batteries in the garage connected to an inverter and a row of top of the range panels on the roof. It’s a modern home with an array of fancy appliances. All the lights are LED’s. It’s a case of 3 W versus 50 for a standard light bulb. His set up cost around R300 000 but it’s an asset he says. “ I am paying about R2000 per month for an investment that will realize a lot more” he says. He is also excited about new battery technology. Elon Musk is making inroads with technology. “ There is a Harvard professor who says one day energy will be free.”


As a banker he is at the vanguard of finding ways to fund a package for solar living that is affordable. He hasn’t looked back – but when he did look up one November night while he was watching the cricket he discovered he was a little light in an island of blackness across from the Northcliff hill to as far as he could see. While his neighbours scurried around for candles he went back to watching the cricket. But does he recommend going off the grid – not yet. I am a banker he says and if it is about cost – the cost of going off grid completely is around R45- 50 000 per KWh. Staying grid tied is R17 000- R20 000.

Press Release:


Off the grid:
What happens when Eskom finally runs out of money is anyone’s guess, but some mavericks already generate their own power. What does it take and is it a viable option? As the country faces another three months of constrained power supply, Carte Blanche meets people living completely off the grid.


Script:


Adios Eskom Final script TX Sunday 25th January 2015

Commentary One
Paul Mikula is a 21st century anachronism

CLUNK CLUNK CLUNK

Paul
Well I am an artist, a blacksmith artist; that is my title.

Commentary Two
But that is not all that is unusual about him. He is forging his metal artwork using this 1930’s German power hammer, it eats electricity but it runs entirely off solar power

VOOSH! BUNG! VOOSH! BUNG!

Derek
I wouldn’t put solar power and forging heavy metal together
Paul
Ya you wouldn’t think it would go together, because I need hard power and people think solar is to heat up a kettle but I needed 3 phase 15 KW power

Commentary Three
For 20 years Paul worked in Hekpoort with no problems
Paul
But then power became a major issue – unreliability for one thing and the expense became ridiculous

Commentary Four
Last year he moved his forge onto the family property on a ridge above Hartebeespoort dam. Paul’s brother in law, Henning, is an architect turned energy specialist who convinced him that combined, the solar panels on the three different family homes would generate enough electricity for his needs.

Up sound solar chicken

Henning lives with his wife and two boys on the first floor. Downstairs he trains architects on green energy. Outside these photovoltaic panels collect energy as direct current – an inverter converts them to AC current for domestic use, and a battery bank stores the energy for up to three rainy days

Henning
The photovoltaic panels are connected to a mini grid, and at the top there these are for the under floor heating – fantastic for the winter…and the balconies for hot showers

Paul
You know what, it’s the most empowering move I have ever made!

VOOSH! VOOSH! VOOSH!

I don’t have to answer to anybody and, well now the powers that be, can go and do their power somewhere else!

Commentary Six
But the powers that be don’t have any power to do somewhere else.
Next week- red, Feb- red March red- ten days ago Eskom told South Africa we must learn to live with load shedding.

Tshedisa Matona
Its not really whether load-shedding is going to be part of our lives its how do we cope with it?

Commentary seven
But bachelor Alister Chabi has realized he doesn’t have to cope with load shedding. He can live without Eskom.

Alister
I came back home and the whole neighborhood was out and the houses in this complex were powered up and I thought ok it is good value for money

Commentary Eight
Alister recently bought a unit in this Midrand complex which offers the best of both worlds. Eskom power when he needs it, but an embedded photovoltaic system when he doesn’t

Alister Chabi
I was a bit concerned about the costs I thought ok how much will a decent, a medium size house cost

Commentary nine
Alister paid an extra R1500 per square meter, adding about another R270 000 onto his bond. For that he has expensive double-glazing, solar panels on the roof, a solar geyser, a bank of batteries in the garage and a home that has eliminated the need for heating and cooling.
Derek
What are the disadvantages?
Alister
I cannot think of any right now
Derek
Really, that good
Alister
Yes it’s that good- I haven’t bothered with Eskom with the connection

Commentary ten
Neither has former banker Pieter Woodhatch who financed his off grid Linden home through his bond

Pieter
My solar solution cost me about R300 000, the energy efficiency – lights and geyser around R50 000 total so around R350 000- so my payments would be about R3500 to R4000 per month

Commentary eleven
But that is still three times more than his Eskom bill would be.

TOAST POPS

But in April power goes up by 13%. And likely, 13% next year, now imagine a 13% compounded return on your money, says Pieter

Pieter
For me it was about saying I am investing in an asset in my house and as a result I can sell the house for more and instead of paying Eskom that money I am using that money to invest in an asset

DEREK LINK
The threat of a total power cuts hang heavy over the country but then along comes a professor who says we can overcome our power issues in under 18 months with no cost to the state

Commentary twelve
At the CSIR Dr Tobias Bischof-Niemz has examined how, in only five years,
German homes and businesses generated the equivalent solar power to what our entire grid has available currently.

Tobias
Germany installed 30 GW from 2009 to 2013 and 30 GW to put that it into perspective that is approximately two thirds of the installed capacity in SA

Commentary Thirteen
Now, provoked by high costs, uncertainty of supply and the plummeting costs of solar panels, businesses across South Africa are also beginning to generate their own power. Tobias does the numbers

Tobias
Five years ago a PV system in SA would have cost you R5 per kw/h whereas the residential tariff was 50 cents, so it wouldn’t make business sense to build a PV system. Today the energy from PV is below R1 per kw/h and the residential tariff is significantly above R1per kw/h

Commentary Fourteen
These rooftop panels reduce this centre’s bill by 20%. At KPMG they have enough panels on their roof to power 87 homes. On weekends, businesses could feed their excess into the grid- and get cash back. Its called a net feed in tariff or NETFIT

Derek to Tobias
So you are proposing a net feed in tariff

Tobias
That is right. It allows you to feed as much energy into the grid as the size of your PV system – it allows you to get cash payments, and it guarantees you an amount that you feed into the grid over the lifetime of the system which is 20 years.

LINK NERSA
Up to now it hasn’t been an option for homeowners and business to feed electricity into the grid but that all about to change

Commentary fifteen
The electricity regulator, Nersa recently released a discussion document that sets the scene for homeowners and businesses to not only to get a reduction on their bills, but also potentially to sell excess energy back into the grid. Nersa’s Thembani Bukula

Thembani
We are planning to have a public hearing in April and after that we should be in a position to make a decision by the end of May or early June

Commentary sixteen
Already the City of Cape Town has a pilot project, where it gets excess power from over 2000 homes, and credits their accounts, but municipalities who make a profit from on selling electricity, are nervous that they will lose out on revenue.

Derek
So you don’t think that trying to please the municipalities would slow down the process

Thembani
I don’t think so, this is going to happen, and in an orderly manner if we manage it this way, or disorderly if it is not managed, and people are allowed to buy the panels and put them on their roofs.

Commentary Seventeen
Inus Druckmeyr is an electrical engineer. He built his family home off the grid 7 years ago and it’s a perfect example of just how much energy a single household can generate

Inus
We would probably be able to sell more than half that we generate
Derek
So if you look at the math over the last 7 years, how do you stand?
Inus
I am definitely up. I am winning. The simple reason is that we went off grid from the word go

Commentary eighteen
Their stone and thatch home east of Pretoria runs multiple appliances- several fridges, more than one TV and the entire security system

Inus
Our approach from the word go was we are not going to punish ourselves to do this – basically we run a stock standard household, we just do it off a different power source

Commentary nineteen
His solar array tracks the warm Pretoria sunshine increasing the yield by 40%.
He heats water with gas and the house with this wood stove. A chandelier, and four hundred low wattage, LED’s light up the home.

Derek
I mean these 400 lights what does that use?
Inus
It uses about 400 watts
Derek
So you are talking 400 watts only using about the same as seven, 60 watt bulbs
Inus
That’s correct

Commentary twenty
When the batteries are charged, energy is diverted to pump water from the borehole to his tank on a nearby hill. All in, Inus system costs around R350 000
but storage is still solar’s Achilles Heal. This battery bank at R150 000 needs replacing every 10 years.

Derek what are the disadvantages here?
Inus
There are none as far as I am concerned, this is the ideal way to live.

Commentary Twenty- one
Ideal it may be, but neither Inus nor Henning recommend going off grid if you are already connected. They suggest a grid tied system of both Eskom and PV power to save costs on expensive batteries. And the cost for a three- bedroom home?

Henning
R120 – R150 000. If you calculate the electricity cost over its lifetime including maintenance – you are at about 80 cents which is very competitive with Eskom which is about R1 40

Derek to Inus
Inus you are an electrical engineer for somebody like myself who doesn’t have a clue where do I start?
Inus
You would consult an expert and the expert would obviously develop a specification that would bring you to a point where you know what you require and what is the reliable stuff out there.

Commentary Twenty-three
Ines advises against trying to do this yourself, if you are unsure consult the electrical engineering association for advice on choosing the right specialist. Its rewarding if you get it right, but many pitfalls along the way if you try and take shortcuts.

THE END duration: 11 minutes 04.

PROMO ONE 10 seconds

Voice over
Goodbye Eskom! Are you considering getting off the grid?
Derek
What are the disadvantages?
Alister
I cannot think of any right now

PROMO TWO 15

Voice over
Soon ordinary households may be able to sell excess electricity into the grid
Derek
So you don’t think that trying to please the municipalities would slow down the process
Thembani Bukula
I don’t think so at this stage. This is going to happen

PROMO THREE 15
Paul
There is no power here, there is no ESKOM – never has been
And it works
It works like a dream
Voice over
High bills and load shedding are prompting South Africans to consider going off the grid

He has a neat row of batteries in the garage connected to an inverter and a row of top of the range panels on the roof. It’s a modern home with an array of fancy appliances. All the lights are LED’s. It’s a case of 3 W versus 50 for a standard light bulb. His set up cost around R300 000 but it’s an asset he says. “ I am paying about R2000 per month for an investment that will realize a lot more” he says. He is also excited about new battery technology. Elon Musk is making inroads with technology. “ There is a Harvard professor who says one day energy will be free.” As a banker he is at the vanguard of finding ways to fund a package for solar living that is affordable. He hasn’t looked back – but when he did look up one November night while he was watching the cricket he discovered he was a little light in an island of blackness across from the Northcliff hill to as far as he could see. While his neighbours scurried around for candles he went back to watching the cricket. But does he recommend going off the grid – not yet. I am a banker he says and if it is about cost – the cost of going off grid completely is around R45- 50 000 per KWh. Staying grid tied is R17 000- R20 000. Script: Adios Eskom Final script TX Sunday 25th January 2015 Commentary One Paul Mikula is a 21st century anachronism CLUNK CLUNK CLUNK Paul Well I am an artist, a blacksmith artist; that is my title. Commentary Two But that is not all that is unusual about him. He is forging his metal artwork using this 1930’s German power hammer, it eats electricity but it runs entirely off solar power VOOSH! BUNG! VOOSH! BUNG! Derek I wouldn’t put solar power and forging heavy metal together Paul Ya you wouldn’t think it would go together, because I need hard power and people think solar is to heat up a kettle but I needed 3 phase 15 KW power Commentary Three For 20 years Paul worked in Hekpoort with no problems Paul But then power became a major issue – unreliability for one thing and the expense became ridiculous Commentary Four Last year he moved his forge onto the family property on a ridge above Hartebeespoort dam. Paul’s brother in law, Henning, is an architect turned energy specialist who convinced him that combined, the solar panels on the three different family homes would generate enough electricity for his needs. Up sound solar chicken Henning lives with his wife and two boys on the first floor. Downstairs he trains architects on green energy. Outside these photovoltaic panels collect energy as direct current – an inverter converts them to AC current for domestic use, and a battery bank stores the energy for up to three rainy days Henning The photovoltaic panels are connected to a mini grid, and at the top there these are for the under floor heating – fantastic for the winter…and the balconies for hot showers Paul You know what, it’s the most empowering move I have ever made! VOOSH! VOOSH! VOOSH! I don’t have to answer to anybody and, well now the powers that be, can go and do their power somewhere else! Commentary Six But the powers that be don’t have any power to do somewhere else. Next week- red, Feb- red March red- ten days ago Eskom told South Africa we must learn to live with load shedding. Tshedisa Matona Its not really whether load-shedding is going to be part of our lives its how do we cope with it? Commentary seven But bachelor Alister Chabi has realized he doesn’t have to cope with load shedding. He can live without Eskom. Alister I came back home and the whole neighborhood was out and the houses in this complex were powered up and I thought ok it is good value for money Commentary Eight Alister recently bought a unit in this Midrand complex which offers the best of both worlds. Eskom power when he needs it, but an embedded photovoltaic system when he doesn’t Alister Chabi I was a bit concerned about the costs I thought ok how much will a decent, a medium size house cost Commentary nine Alister paid an extra R1500 per square meter, adding about another R270 000 onto his bond. For that he has expensive double-glazing, solar panels on the roof, a solar geyser, a bank of batteries in the garage and a home that has eliminated the need for heating and cooling. Derek What are the disadvantages? Alister I cannot think of any right now Derek Really, that good Alister Yes it’s that good- I haven’t bothered with Eskom with the connection Commentary ten Neither has former banker Pieter Woodhatch who financed his off grid Linden home through his bond Pieter My solar solution cost me about R300 000, the energy efficiency – lights and geyser around R50 000 total so around R350 000- so my payments would be about R3500 to R4000 per month Commentary eleven But that is still three times more than his Eskom bill would be. TOAST POPS But in April power goes up by 13%. And likely, 13% next year, now imagine a 13% compounded return on your money, says Pieter Pieter For me it was about saying I am investing in an asset in my house and as a result I can sell the house for more and instead of paying Eskom that money I am using that money to invest in an asset DEREK LINK The threat of a total power cuts hang heavy over the country but then along comes a professor who says we can overcome our power issues in under 18 months with no cost to the state Commentary twelve At the CSIR Dr Tobias Bischof-Niemz has examined how, in only five years, German homes and businesses generated the equivalent solar power to what our entire grid has available currently. Tobias Germany installed 30 GW from 2009 to 2013 and 30 GW to put that it into perspective that is approximately two thirds of the installed capacity in SA Commentary Thirteen Now, provoked by high costs, uncertainty of supply and the plummeting costs of solar panels, businesses across South Africa are also beginning to generate their own power. Tobias does the numbers Tobias Five years ago a PV system in SA would have cost you R5 per kw/h whereas the residential tariff was 50 cents, so it wouldn’t make business sense to build a PV system. Today the energy from PV is below R1 per kw/h and the residential tariff is significantly above R1per kw/h Commentary Fourteen These rooftop panels reduce this centre’s bill by 20%. At KPMG they have enough panels on their roof to power 87 homes. On weekends, businesses could feed their excess into the grid- and get cash back. Its called a net feed in tariff or NETFIT Derek to Tobias So you are proposing a net feed in tariff Tobias That is right. It allows you to feed as much energy into the grid as the size of your PV system – it allows you to get cash payments, and it guarantees you an amount that you feed into the grid over the lifetime of the system which is 20 years. LINK NERSA Up to now it hasn’t been an option for homeowners and business to feed electricity into the grid but that all about to change Commentary fifteen The electricity regulator, Nersa recently released a discussion document that sets the scene for homeowners and businesses to not only to get a reduction on their bills, but also potentially to sell excess energy back into the grid. Nersa’s Thembani Bukula Thembani We are planning to have a public hearing in April and after that we should be in a position to make a decision by the end of May or early June Commentary sixteen Already the City of Cape Town has a pilot project, where it gets excess power from over 2000 homes, and credits their accounts, but municipalities who make a profit from on selling electricity, are nervous that they will lose out on revenue. Derek So you don’t think that trying to please the municipalities would slow down the process Thembani I don’t think so, this is going to happen, and in an orderly manner if we manage it this way, or disorderly if it is not managed, and people are allowed to buy the panels and put them on their roofs. Commentary Seventeen Inus Druckmeyr is an electrical engineer. He built his family home off the grid 7 years ago and it’s a perfect example of just how much energy a single household can generate Inus We would probably be able to sell more than half that we generate Derek So if you look at the math over the last 7 years, how do you stand? Inus I am definitely up. I am winning. The simple reason is that we went off grid from the word go Commentary eighteen Their stone and thatch home east of Pretoria runs multiple appliances- several fridges, more than one TV and the entire security system Inus Our approach from the word go was we are not going to punish ourselves to do this – basically we run a stock standard household, we just do it off a different power source Commentary nineteen His solar array tracks the warm Pretoria sunshine increasing the yield by 40%. He heats water with gas and the house with this wood stove. A chandelier, and four hundred low wattage, LED’s light up the home. Derek I mean these 400 lights what does that use? Inus It uses about 400 watts Derek So you are talking 400 watts only using about the same as seven, 60 watt bulbs Inus That’s correct Commentary twenty When the batteries are charged, energy is diverted to pump water from the borehole to his tank on a nearby hill. All in, Inus system costs around R350 000 but storage is still solar’s Achilles Heal. This battery bank at R150 000 needs replacing every 10 years. Derek what are the disadvantages here? Inus There are none as far as I am concerned, this is the ideal way to live. Commentary Twenty- one Ideal it may be, but neither Inus nor Henning recommend going off grid if you are already connected. They suggest a grid tied system of both Eskom and PV power to save costs on expensive batteries. And the cost for a three- bedroom home? Henning R120 – R150 000. If you calculate the electricity cost over its lifetime including maintenance – you are at about 80 cents which is very competitive with Eskom which is about R1 40 Derek to Inus Inus you are an electrical engineer for somebody like myself who doesn’t have a clue where do I start? Inus You would consult an expert and the expert would obviously develop a specification that would bring you to a point where you know what you require and what is the reliable stuff out there. Commentary Twenty-three Ines advises against trying to do this yourself, if you are unsure consult the electrical engineering association for advice on choosing the right specialist. Its rewarding if you get it right, but many pitfalls along the way if you try and take shortcuts. THE END duration: 11 minutes 04. PROMO ONE 10 seconds Voice over Goodbye Eskom! Alister I cannot think of any right now PROMO TWO 15 Voice over Soon ordinary households may be able to sell excess electricity into the grid Derek So you don’t think that trying to please the municipalities would slow down the process Thembani Bukula I don’t think so at this stage. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Eskom runs out of money at the end of the month what happens then is anyones guess, but for those mavericks who are living off the grid they will barely notice - what does it take and is it an option
metadata.Summary: Carte Blanche meets the early adopters who have gone off the grid and finds out if it is a good idea as the country faces a year of constrained supply
metadata.Further information: Adios Eskom At the end of the month Eskom will run out of money. Just how that will affect the country hardly bears thinking about, but there is a small group of people that probably wont even notice. They are the mavericks, the early adopters – those who have chosen to get off the grid and generate their own power. How did they do it? What did it cost them? As we look on from our darkened homes with envy, we wonder if we too can make the leap and say Adios Eskom! Inus Dreckmeyr lives East of Pretoria in a beautiful home with his wife and family and all the creature comforts you can imagine. Six years ago he built him home, designed to keep warm in winter and cool in summer. He has custom built a solar array that moves with the sun, increasing his power by about 70 %. He has a room full of batteries which store the excess energy he will need at night and when they are full the energy diverts to a water pump that pumps borehole water to a tank on the hill to give the family enough water pressure for bathing and showering At the time Inus spent around R600 000 to equip his home. But now as the cost of PV has dropped by about 80% he believes it will cost about half of that. At the top of the hill overlooking Hartebeespoort dam is the property of the Henning family. The modest house that looks like it is painted with an Ndebele design is in fact a means to attract heat in winter and repel it in summer. This is the home of architect Professor Holm who went off the grid way back in 1974. His hot water comes from a glass encased black box that heats up and pushes itself into an insulated tank that provides the pressure for showering. But this fascination with solar runs in the family and his son Henning now spends his days helping big corporate clients reduce their dependency on Eskom. His office and home are flanked by Solar panels – in winter heated water runs under his floors giving him underfloor heating. Everything is connected via a computer so at any given time he can see exactly what is happening on the property. To power the three homes and a business he has built a mini grid with inverter and a roomful of batteries. It’s an impressive operation that has cost in the region of R900 000. The business belongs to his brother in law, Paul, a blacksmith who makes beautiful cast iron art. Paul was fed up. He says he endured 28 days with no power in Hekpoort in 2014. His friends are selling up businesses and moving elsewhere. Paul decided to take his chance with solar and moved his forge onto the property recently. It’s a strange sight to see lumbering old German machines from the 30’s shaping red hot pieces of iron into beautiful artwork and remembering its all being powered from just a few solar panels on old man Henning’s rooftop. But ask Henning Holm if we should get off the grid and he will tell you no, it’s still too expensive. What you should do is get a hybrid system he says. That way you can get the best of both worlds. He will explain this system to Derek. But if you decide you want to make the leap and you don’t have R300 000 lying around what do you do? Will the banks lend a hand? “ I used to have a round head, now its flat” says Brett Petzer who has spent the last four years knocking on the doors of the top four banks.“ They weren’t interested” he says and the green bank refused to cross the threshold. Nevertheless Brett has developed an off grid townhouse development in Midrand. “ The whites weren’t interested he said, but my black clients said this is the future and bought into the development and the concept” He will introduce us to Mr Stockbroker who runs everything in this stylish development off solar panels, except his Jacuzzi. And his bill from Eskom: Zero! THE GERMAN EXAMPLE As the Germans can show – living off solar panels not only provides enough for our own needs, there is usually plenty to spare. In an effort to go renewable the German government introduced incentives for their citizens to sell energy back to the grid and in so doing Germans put up solar PV panels everywhere. They paid a lot for their energy, but in a few short years Germany has as much solar PV energy as the entire South African energy grid. “ In terms of solar Germany decided they would buy a Mercedes S class because they wanted renewables even though they were expensive. As a result of that Germany pushed down the price of solar PV to such an extent that now South Africa can do the same thing but at the price of a VW Golf” that is the message from the CSIR’s Dr Tobias Bischoff Niemz. Dr Bischoff Niemz is an expert in the field and is advising NERSA on how to do the same thing here. The exciting news for jaded Eskom customers is that last month NERSA issued a discussion document. Until now feeding energy into the grid has been illegal in South Africa. But as Eskom battles to keep the lights on NERSA is taking a tentative step towards opening up the market. Put up a system on your roof and you may either be able to sell on your excess energy or get credits for what you do use – thereby reducing your bill. It called net metering or NET FIT (FEED IN TARIFF) But before you get too excited – it’s not yet law and there is a large and powerful lobby against this in the form of the municipalities and the METRO’S who Dr Bischoff Niemz says will go bankrupt if too many homeowners and businesses decide to ditch the grid. A huge portion of the metro and munics revenue comes from the mark up on electricity, which is then used to cross subsidize other municipal functions. But the CSIR doctor has a plan. “ Don’t let this happen under the radar,” he says. He suggests that a central purchasing agency buys your energy back at say 70cents per kwh. We import our electricity at about R1 30 per kwh. He also suggests that the agency guarantee a pay back for about 20 years, which will mean banks may lend to home owners knowing that they are likely to get their money back. We need to do this right he says. If you do one thing wrong the whole thing can fail. In Spain the whole experiment failed because they did it wrong. “ I am less excited about this net metering than others” says Peter Woodhatch an ex banker, skeptically. “ Say one invests in a lot of PV and then at a point government decides they don’t want your energy anymore. Then you lose your return on investment.” Peter is another young maverick. His new home in Linden is built and designed to keep the temperature relatively constant and when Eskom said they wanted R20 000 for a connection from the street to his gate he decided to get off the grid instead. Peter was prompted by what he calls comfort. Too many friends and family members had spent hours fighting with ESKOM over ridiculous bills. He says he has neither time nor the will to spend hours fighting the city over incorrect billing. Peter has a gas geyser and stove and an electric oven. He has a neat row of batteries in the garage connected to an inverter and a row of top of the range panels on the roof. It’s a modern home with an array of fancy appliances. All the lights are LED’s. It’s a case of 3 W versus 50 for a standard light bulb. His set up cost around R300 000 but it’s an asset he says. “ I am paying about R2000 per month for an investment that will realize a lot more” he says. He is also excited about new battery technology. Elon Musk is making inroads with technology. “ There is a Harvard professor who says one day energy will be free.” As a banker he is at the vanguard of finding ways to fund a package for solar living that is affordable. He hasn’t looked back – but when he did look up one November night while he was watching the cricket he discovered he was a little light in an island of blackness across from the Northcliff hill to as far as he could see. While his neighbours scurried around for candles he went back to watching the cricket. But does he recommend going off the grid – not yet. I am a banker he says and if it is about cost – the cost of going off grid completely is around R45- 50 000 per KWh. Staying grid tied is R17 000- R20 000.
